product_id.name: product_id
product_id.description:
Surrogate key for the product. Joins to `products.product_id`, and is
the id_column the search service returns so a citation can be resolved
back to a catalogue row.

product_name.name: product_name
product_name.description:
The menu item's name as printed on the receipt. Carried here as the
search service's title_column, so a citation names the item rather
than its key.

product_type.name: product_type
product_type.description:
Whether the item is food or drink. Carried here as a search ATTRIBUTE,
which is what makes it filterable in a search request -- the same
column is an enum DIMENSION over on `products`, for the analyst path.

dietary_class.name: dietary_class
dietary_class.description:
Whether the item is vegan, vegetarian or omnivore. A search ATTRIBUTE,
which is what makes it FILTERABLE in a search request.

AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED FROM THE PROSE. The description already says
"Vegetarian." or "Not vegetarian.", and an ILIKE over that text is a
filter that INVERTS ITSELF the first time somebody writes "not
suitable for vegetarians" -- the substring "vegetarian" matches both
readings. The class is a column because the answer must not depend on
how the sentence was phrased.

AND IT EXISTS BECAUSE SEMANTIC SEARCH ALONE GOT THIS WRONG, measured
rather than assumed. With diet expressed only in the prose, the query
"vegan items with no dairy" returned FOUR VEGETARIAN-BUT-DAIRY items
and NONE of the three vegan ones: the embedding puts "Vegetarian." and
"Vegetarian and vegan." close together and cannot be asked to exclude
one. With this column as an attribute the same intent returns exactly
the three vegan items. A closed set belongs in a filter, not in a
vector.

product_description.name: product_description
product_description.description:
Long-form menu copy: what is in the item, and whether it is
vegetarian. THE INDEXED COLUMN. This is the only column in the project
that carries prose, and the only reason `product_docs` exists.
